transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-30
Time: 16:00 UTC / 09:00 PT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Jared (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Carlos (Redwood Solutions), Elena (Moontrail), Marco (Moontrail Infra), Tanya (Moontrail Security), Owen (Moontrail PM)
Shared links: https://redwood.ai/partners/deck (Redwood partner deck), spreadsheet: https://redwood.ai/benchmarks/partner-eval.xlsx (benchmarks)

[00:00:00] Jared: Hi everyone, thanks for taking the time. I'm Jared from Redwood inference, AE on the partnerships team. With me is Priya, our systems and private deployment SE, and Carlos who helps run partner ops.
[00:00:12] Elena: Hey Jared, thanks. I'm Elena, I run cloud partnerships at Moontrail. We are excited to understand how Redwood could onramp our managed SaaS offering to GPU capacity and also support customers that need on-prem options.
[00:00:22] Marco: Hi, Marco here, infra eng. Quick note we're evaluating both hosted on cloud and a self-hosted on-prem suite for high security customers.
[00:00:28] Priya: Great to meet you all. We try to cover both sides — low fric hosted API for most customers, and a private package that runs inside a VPC or even on-prem for regulated customers.
[00:00:38] Owen: I just joined — product PM, curious how integration footprint looks.
[00:00:42] Carlos: Before we dive, can you share a little bit about Moontrail's top-level use cases and any constraints — e.g., latency needs, model sizes, compliance?
[00:00:50] Elena: Sure. Moontrail offers a multi-tenant SaaS for logistics optimization, and we've started adding an LLM layer for planning and natural language interfaces. Typical model runs are chat-style, with both short queries and longer prompts up to 2k tokens. We're using a mix of open models and a few fine-tuned variants.
[00:01:08] Elena: Key constraints: data residency for EU customers, SOC2-like audits, and for some large shippers we need on-prem or VPC-only access. Latency targets are 200-400ms p95 for short prompts, and throughput for batch scoring of planning candidates is important. Cost is obviously a factor.
[00:01:25] Priya: Good context. For latency p95 at that range for short prompts, we typically route to low-latency hosted capacity with preference for dedicated pools. For batch scoring you can use dedicated or reserved capacity, or a CPU-optimized path for offline scoring.
[00:01:41] Marco: On the on-prem side, what does your private deployment look like? Is it a single-node package or multi-node cluster? Any hard requirements for Kubernetes, or can it run on our own VM images behind a firewall?
[00:01:53] Priya: Our private package has two flavors: a lightweight VPC appliance for customers who want the Redwood control plane but data path inside customer infra, and a fully self-hosted on-prem bundle which is Kubernetes-optional. The fully self-hosted still needs a node manager and a container runtime; we can support k8s, or a docker-compose style on bare metal for small clusters. We also have an on-prem package tested on standard GPU servers (A100 and H100).
[00:02:16] Marco: H100 support is great to hear — a lot of our data center partners are moving that way. How about mixed GPU pools? Some customers will want A100 for cost optimization, others H100 for latency.
[00:02:26] Priya: We do mixed pools and smart routing — you can set policies to route by latency SLO or cost. We also support model variants (quantized vs fp16) so the system can fallback to cheaper variants if capacity is constrained.
[00:02:38] Tanya: From security, we need to understand auth and audit. Do you integrate with SAML/SSO, and how granular is RBAC? Also KMS for key material?
[00:02:47] Carlos: Yes, we integrate with SAML/SSO and OIDC for hosted customers, and in Private deployment you can plug in your KMS/HSM. RBAC is per-team and per-route; audit logs are available for every call with token-level details. We can retain logs per your retention policy; that's configurable.
[00:03:03] Owen: What's the typical integration touchpoints for our product engineers? Is it a REST endpoint, SDK, or more embedded runtime?
[00:03:10] Priya: Primary integration is a simple REST/SDK interface for generation, embeddings, and reranking. For customers embedding Redwood inside a managed SaaS we also provide a connector pattern that manages auth and routing so your app talks to a local sidecar that forwards to Redwood runtime.
[00:03:24] Elena: That sidecar sounds promising — we'd like to keep things as thin as possible for our customers. Can you talk about model onboarding — we run a few fine-tuned models; would you host them or do we bring our own?
[00:03:34] Priya: Both options. For hosted customers we can host and serve your fine-tuned artifacts, or you can bring them into the private package. We have recommendations for quantization and kernel tuning. Also worth noting: for private deployments we give tooling to compile kernels for your target hardware.
[00:03:50] Marco: Any existing partner integrations with SaaS platforms? Curious about operational patterns and what we should expect during pilot.
[00:03:58] Carlos: We've run onramps with a handful of SaaS partners — typical pilot is 4–6 weeks: we share a benchmark harness, run representative traffic, capture latency/cost, and then iterate on batching/kv caching configs. We often do a small dedicated footprint for the pilot.
[00:04:15] Elena: Sounds aligned with what we'd want. For the pilot we need a simple success criteria: latency p95 under 400ms for short prompts, cost per 1k tokens under a threshold we'll share, and a security checklist with SSO + audit.
[00:04:28] Jared: Good — we'll capture that as the success criteria. We'll also share a partner benchmark spreadsheet so you can populate samples.
[00:04:35] [00:04:36] (crosstalk) Marco: Quick Q — how intrusive is the performance instrumentation? We can't have heavy telemetry in our production path.
[00:04:43] Priya: Instrumentation is lightweight — token-level tracing is optional; default is aggregates and per-route latency. For private installs you control telemetry endpoints.
[00:04:52] Tanya: Regarding compliance, we need SOC2 alignment and an option for offline log storage. Is your SOC2 in place?
[00:04:59] Carlos: Yes, Redwood is SOC2 Type II. For private customers we can certify the package with your auditor; logs can be exported to your SIEM or retained in your vault. We'll share our security pack after the call.
[00:05:10] Elena: Are there any network egress concerns? Some partners want no outbound connections from their air-gapped clusters.
[00:05:17] Priya: For fully air-gapped installs we can ship an offline bundle. That requires a bit more ops time for handshake and cert provisioning, but yes it's supported. The VPC appliance is more lightweight — it keeps control plane traffic minimal.
[00:05:29] Owen: On the commercial side, how do partner programs usually work? Any revenue share or referral?
[00:05:35] Jared: We have a few partner tracks — referral with credits, reseller with co-sell margins, and strategic integrations with joint go-to-market. We can tailor an agreement depending on volume and support needs. Carlos will follow up with program details.
[00:05:48] Marco: Back to technical — batching and KV cache sound important. Can you explain how prefix caching works and whether it affects correctness?
[00:05:56] Priya: Sure. Prefix/KV caching stores computed past key/values for repeated prefixes so subsequent calls with the same context avoid recomputing. It's safe for deterministic models; for models with sampling it's used carefully and can be disabled per route. For your planning use-case, we often cache the system prompt and static context, which gives big TPS wins with no correctness change.
[00:06:19] Marco: Great. And how do you handle model fallbacks during outages — is there an auto-failover to smaller quantized variants?
[00:06:26] Priya: Yes, you can define fallback chains. If a high-performance H100-backed variant is unavailable, the router can fall back to an A100 or quantized variant. You can set threshold policies so fallbacks only happen under certain error rates or latency spikes.
[00:06:39] Elena: For our EU customers, do you provide regional hosting and data residency?
[00:06:44] Jared: Yes, we have EU regions and can pin customer workloads to specific regions. For Private deployments you keep data in your DCs.
[00:06:52] Tanya: On the certs and key management, we need to enforce customer-managed KMS for encryption at rest. Is that supported?
[00:06:58] Carlos: Supported. In Private, you mount your KMS/HSM credentials and we never hold the master keys. For hosted we offer integrations with cloud KMS providers, and for enterprise we can do HSM integrations.
[00:07:10] [00:07:11] Marco: Any gotchas with CUDA versions or driver compatibility? We've seen issues with older stacks.
[00:07:16] Priya: We publish supported drivers and CUDA matrix — for H100 we recommend the newer runtimes and specific kernel builds. We also provide container images with pinned drivers to reduce drift.
[00:07:26] Owen: For our product roadmap we might want an SDK that hides tokenization differences across models. Do you help normalize outputs?
[00:07:33] Priya: We provide SDKs and model adapters that normalize tokenization and stream outputs consistently. For model-specific quirks we add compatibility layers in the SDK.
[00:07:41] Elena: Can you share an example of a past onboarding where an SI had to handle on-prem customers? What's the timeline?
[00:07:48] Carlos: Typical timeline: discovery + scoping (1–2 weeks), pilot provisioning (2–4 weeks), pilot run (4 weeks), then rollout planning. For on-prem air-gapped installs add 2–3 weeks for validation and cert exchange.
[00:08:03] Marco: Licensing — do we buy reserved capacity or per-token?
[00:08:07] Jared: Options: hosted per-token or per-hour pricing, reserved capacity for Dedicated, and a license + support model for Private. Partners often start on a hosted trial then commit to reserved or private when volume justifies it.
[00:08:20] Tanya: Do you provide any automated compliance attestation or penetration tests for private installs?
[00:08:26] Priya: We provide artifacts (SOC2 report, pen test summaries) and can run a joint pen test with your security team. For private installs we recommend an initial security validation run.
[00:08:36] Elena: Ok, let's talk pilot scope. We'd like Redwood to run an eval on a representative subset of our traffic: mixed chat queries and batch scoring. We want to measure p95 latency, throughput, and cost per scoring run.
[00:08:48] Jared: Good. We'll send a benchmark harness and suggested traffic sample format. Marco, can you provide a 2-week traffic dump and token distribution?
[00:08:56] Marco: Yes, I can scrub PII and provide anonymized token traces. We'll also include prompt templates.
[00:09:02] Priya: Once we have the sample, we'll run it on a small dedicated footprint — usually 2–4 GPUs depending on model — and tune batching and cache settings. We'll share a report with recommendations (quantization, routing, autoscale settings).
[00:09:15] Owen: Curious about SLA — what's typical for Dedicated customers?
[00:09:19] Jared: Dedicated comes with an SLA on uptime and latency SLOs; we can scope the exact numbers in an enterprise contract based on capacity.
[00:09:26] [00:09:27] Tanya: One last security Q — audit log retention: can we guarantee retention windows and export formats?
[00:09:32] Carlos: Yes, logs can be exported in JSONL to your S3, SIEM, or retained for X days depending on tier. We can also sign logs for tamper-evidence if that's required.
[00:09:42] Elena: Sounds promising. As next steps, let's get the deck and benchmark sheet, and we'll align internal stakeholders.
[00:09:49] Jared: Great. Recap of next steps: Jared sends partner deck and benchmark link; Marco provides token samples; Tanya provides security checklist; Priya will draft possible on-prem packaging options and timeline. We'll schedule a technical deep dive for the private package next week.
[00:10:03] Carlos: I'll also include partner program terms and a short pilot budget outline.
[00:10:08] Elena: Thanks everyone. We want to move quickly — target pilot start mid-April if possible.
[00:10:13] Jared: We'll aim for that. Thanks all.
[00:10:18] (meeting ends)

Notes about transcript quality: there are occasional transcription errors around acronyms (V P C transcribed as V P C, K V cache as K V cash) and some proper nouns may be slightly off. The technical details should be validated in follow-ups.
